blocks.title: What the interviewer is really testing
blocks.text: LeetCode 642 is the *toy*. The real question is: **can you turn every prefix into an O(1) lookup without drowning in storage and invalidation cost?** Anyone can DFS a trie on every keystroke. Strong candidates precompute, defend the storage-vs-latency trade-off, then explain what breaks when that trie no longer fits on one box and when writes arrive concurrently.
The problem

Design a search autocomplete system seeded with historical data, then driven character-by-character. You are given `sentences` and parallel `times` — how often each sentence was searched in the past. After construction the system processes a stream via `input(c)`. If `c` is a normal character (letter or space), append it to the current prefix and return the top 3 hottest sentences with that prefix. Hotness is frequency descending, lexicographic ascending as tie-break. If `c` is `#`, the current prefix is a completed search: record it (increment its count by 1, or insert it if new), reset the current prefix to empty, and return an empty list. The current prefix always starts empty, and `#` never appears inside a sentence.

items: `AutocompleteSystem(String[] sentences, int[] times)` — build initial index. `sentences.length <= 100` and each sentence length `<= 100` in the LeetCode scope; production scope is billions of distinct queries.
`List<String> input(char c)` — if `c == '#'` persist current query and reset; else advance one character in the prefix and return up to 3 matches.
Ordering contract is strict: higher `times` first, then ASCII / lexicographic order. Get this wrong and every test with ties fails.
Characters are lowercase letters plus space (`27` symbols). That small alphabet is why a trie works — say it explicitly.

blocks.text: Clarify before you code
Do not start with the trie. The interviewer grades whether you pin down persistence, ranking, and scale first. Five questions separate a LeetCode recitation from a design discussion.

items.title: Where does frequency come from?
items.text: Are `times` immutable history, or does every `#` mutate global counts? LeetCode says mutate. Production says distinguish personal history from global popularity. Agree: `#` increments a global counter that immediately affects future rankings.

items.title: What is k and is it fixed?
items.text: LeetCode fixes `k = 3`. Real products use 5-10 and per-surface tuning. Fix `k` as a config constant so precomputation stays bounded, and state that larger `k` linearly inflates every trie node.

items.title: Single node or distributed?
items.text: Ask whether the follow-up expects one-machine concurrency or a multi-shard service. Your answer changes from a lock around a trie to prefix sharding plus an offline aggregation pipeline. Ask now.

items.title: Latency and freshness targets?
items.text: Autocomplete must respond in tens of milliseconds per keystroke or it feels broken. Freshness can lag by minutes for global trends but personal history should reflect instantly. That split justifies a fast read path plus an asynchronous write path.

items.title: Input alphabet and normalisation?
items.text: Case-sensitive? Punctuation? Unicode? Empty prefix? For the interview assume exactly `a-z` plus space and no normalisation, but name the boundary where a real system would lowercase, trim, and collapse whitespace before lookup.

blocks.text: Approach 1 — brute force scan and sort

Keep a hash map from sentence to count. On every normal character, scan all sentences, filter by `startsWith(prefix)`, sort matches by the ranking rule, take 3. On `#`, bump the map and reset. It is five lines, obviously correct, and exactly what you should describe first so you can reject it for concrete reasons. The trade-off is brutal: zero index maintenance cost in exchange for paying full scan cost on the hottest path — every keystroke.

items: Read cost is `O(N * L)` per keystroke where `N` is sentence count and `L` is average length, plus `O(M log M)` sort over `M` matches. At `N = 10^9` web queries this is dead on arrival.
No prefix sharing: `inter`, `interview`, and `interviewer` are compared independently every time, repeating the same prefix checks the trie would do once.
Sorting on read wastes work. The top-3 for `i love` does not change between `i lov` and `i love` unless a write intervened, yet brute force recomputes it from scratch.
It teaches the right lesson: autocomplete is read-heavy (hundreds of reads per write), so any design must shift work from read to write, even if that makes writes heavier.

blocks.text: Real design — precompute top-k at every trie node

Build a trie over the 27-character alphabet. The root represents the empty prefix; each edge consumes one character; each node represents one distinct prefix. Every node stores the top-k hottest sentences in its subtree, maintained on every insert. Reads then become trie descent only: advance one edge per character and return the cached list — no scan, no sort. The trade-off you must state: you buy `O(1)`-per-keystroke reads with extra memory (`k` sentence references per prefix node) and heavier writes (`O(P * k log k)` to refresh every prefix of an inserted sentence, where `P` is sentence length). For autocomplete that is the correct side of the trade because reads outnumber writes by orders of magnitude.

blocks.title: Read path vs write path
blocks.caption: Reads descend the trie and hit cached top-k. Writes go through ingestion and refresh every prefix node.
blocks.code:
flowchart LR
  User[User keystroke] --> LB[Load balancer]
  LB --> Svc[Autocomplete service]
  Svc --> Cache[Prefix cache]
  Cache -- hit --> Resp[Top-k response]
  Cache -- miss --> Shard[Trie shard by prefix]
  Shard --> Resp
  Typed[Completed query on hash] --> Log[Write log]
  Log --> Agg[Aggregator]
  Agg --> Shard

blocks.text: In production this splits into two paths. The synchronous read path is sharded by prefix hash so all queries for `inter*` land on the same shard, fronted by a small LRU of hot prefixes — the top 10k prefixes serve the majority of traffic. The asynchronous write path appends completed queries to a log, aggregates counts offline, and pushes refreshed top-k lists to the owning shards. That is why personal history is applied synchronously on the request path (small, per-user) while global counts update with a delay of seconds to minutes: freshness where it matters, batch efficiency where it scales. The trade-off is eventual consistency of global rankings in exchange for bounded write amplification.

blocks.title: In-memory index shape
blocks.caption: Each trie node caches its hottest sentences so input() never searches.

blocks.text: Why the node stores references, not copies

Each node's `hot` list holds at most `k = 3` sentence identities ordered by the ranking rule, plus access to a global frequency map. You never duplicate full strings per node in the interview implementation — nodes point at shared strings. That keeps memory at `O(T + U * k)` where `T` is total trie nodes and `U` is distinct prefixes, instead of `O(U * k * L)`. The cost is that a frequency bump must revisit every prefix node of that sentence to re-sort its tiny `k`-list. With `k = 3` the sort is constant time, so the write stays `O(P)` trie steps. State this explicitly: tiny `k` is what makes per-node caching affordable; if the product ever asks for `k = 100`, this design needs rethinking.

blocks.text: Concurrency and the hardest follow-up — leaving one box

On one machine the hazard is the `#` write racing concurrent `input` reads. The cursor (`current` plus `cursor` pointer) is per-connection state and must never be shared — each session gets its own. The shared structures are the trie and the frequency map. The pragmatic answer: guard the trie with a read-write lock (many concurrent descents, exclusive insert) or a per-node lock for insert-heavy workloads, and return a defensive copy of `hot` so a reader never observes a list being re-sorted mid-read. Copy-on-write of the tiny `hot` list is cheap and removes the most common race. At distributed scale the follow-up is sharding plus freshness. Shard the trie by first character or by prefix hash so each shard owns a disjoint prefix range; replicate hot shards and front them with a CDN or edge cache keyed by prefix. Completed queries flow through a durable log into a streaming counter, and only aggregated deltas refresh shards every few seconds. The trade-off: reads stay local to one shard with no fan-out, but cross-shard ranking (global top-k across shards) is approximate until the next aggregation cycle — acceptable because autocomplete tolerates slightly stale global order.

items: Per-session cursor: never store `current` in a singleton service bean. One instance per user session, or pass it as a request parameter.
Hot-prefix invalidation: bumping `i love you` must refresh nodes `i`, `i `, `i l`, ... — batch these refreshes or a viral query causes a write storm down one shard.
Thundering herd on viral prefixes: cache the top prefixes at the edge with a short TTL rather than letting every keystroke hit the shard.
Personal vs global: layer per-user history (small trie or recent list, applied at request time) over the shared global trie so personalisation needs no global lock.

blocks.title: The trap most candidates walk into
blocks.text: DFS-ing the subtree on every `input` to collect candidates passes LeetCode but fails the interview the moment the follow-up mentions scale. Say upfront why you cache top-k at the node: keystrokes are 100x more frequent than completed queries, so write amplification is cheaper than read amplification. If you start with DFS, state it as a scaffold and replace it before the interviewer asks.
Follow-ups to have ready

items.title: Real-time vs batch freshness?
items.text: Answer: personal `#` applies instantly to that user's view; global counts propagate via the log every N seconds. Trade-off is immediate personal relevance against bounded global write load.

items.title: Typo tolerance and fuzzy match?
items.text: Answer: keep the exact trie for the sub-50ms path, add a parallel edit-distance-1 expansion or a symspell index for the miss path. Trade-off is recall against latency — never put fuzzy search on the critical path.

items.title: Trending and time decay?
items.text: Answer: replace raw counts with decayed scores (count in last hour weighted higher) computed offline. Trade-off is a background recompute job against static frequencies going stale during events.

items.title: Personalisation and privacy?
items.text: Answer: per-user boost layer merged at rank time, stored separately with TTL and deletion support. Trade-off is extra merge cost per request against one global index leaking one user's queries to another.

items.title: Delete and moderation?
items.text: Answer: tombstone the sentence, decrement or zero its frequency, and refresh its prefix chain. Trade-off is that delete is as expensive as insert — there is no cheap removal from precomputed lists.

blocks.text: Edge cases to state unprompted

items: `#` on an empty prefix: record nothing, just reset. Otherwise you insert an empty sentence into the root.
Unknown prefix mid-stream: once `cursor` becomes null, all further characters return `[]` until `#` — but keep accumulating `current` so the full string is recorded.
Tie-break order: equal frequencies must return lexicographic ascending. Write the comparator before the trie.
Spaces are characters: `i love` and `ilove` are different prefixes; do not trim or split.
Repeated `#` completions of the same new sentence must promote it through every prefix node's top-3 over time — good test of `refresh`.
Prefix that is also a full sentence: node must list the sentence itself alongside longer extensions, ranked by heat.

blocks.title: 45-minute plan
blocks.text: Minutes 0-5: pin API, ranking rule, and single-vs-distributed scope. 5-12: name brute force and kill it with `O(N)` per keystroke. 12-25: build the trie with per-node top-3 and the comparator — write the Java. 25-33: handle `#`, null cursor, and empty-prefix edge cases live. 33-42: concurrency (session cursor, RW-lock, copied lists) then scale-out (prefix shards, edge cache, log-backed aggregation). 42-45: close with two follow-ups you can sketch — decay and personalisation — each with its trade-off.
